title: Acids, Bases and Salts
description: The reactions of acids with metals, bases and carbonates; indicator colours and the pH scale; the neutralisation ionic equation; preparing a pure soluble salt; and the solubility rules — Core content for Cambridge IGCSE Chemistry 0620.

notes.heading: The Three Reactions of Acids
notes.body:
You met these at KS3; at 0620 you must name the salt product and state the observations precisely.

📌 The three general reactions
• acid + **metal** → salt + hydrogen
• acid + **base** (metal oxide or hydroxide) → salt + water
• acid + **carbonate** → salt + water + carbon dioxide

🔑 Naming the salt
The ACID decides the second word of the salt's name: hydrochloric acid → a **chloride**, sulfuric acid → a **sulfate**, nitric acid → a **nitrate**. The metal supplies the first word.

💡 Worked Examples
• Mg + H₂SO₄ → MgSO₄ + H₂ (magnesium sulfate; bubbles of hydrogen)
• CuO + 2HCl → CuCl₂ + H₂O (copper(II) chloride; black solid dissolves)
• CaCO₃ + 2HNO₃ → Ca(NO₃)₂ + H₂O + CO₂ (calcium nitrate; effervescence)

⚠️ Common Mistake
Writing 'salt + hydrogen + water' for a metal reaction. Metals give salt + hydrogen ONLY — no water. Water appears with bases (neutralisation) and carbonates.

📎 Key Points to Remember
• Only metals ABOVE hydrogen in the reactivity series react with dilute acids (Cu, Ag, Au do not).
• Gas tests: H₂ gives a squeaky pop with a lighted splint; CO₂ turns limewater milky.

notes.heading: Indicators: Litmus, Methyl Orange, Thymolphthalein
notes.body:
0620 requires the colours of three named indicators in acidic and alkaline solutions — learn them as a table.

📌 The required colours
• **Litmus**: red in acid, blue in alkali.
• **Methyl orange**: red in acid, yellow in alkali.
• **Thymolphthalein**: colourless in acid, blue in alkali.

🔑 What an indicator result proves
A single indicator only tells you acid-or-alkali, not HOW acidic. Two different acids both turn litmus red, whether pH 1 or pH 6. To pin down a pH value you need universal indicator (next note).

💡 Worked Example
A solution turns methyl orange red and thymolphthalein colourless. Both results say 'acidic' — consistent, but you still cannot tell a strong acid from a weak one without universal indicator or a pH meter.

⚠️ Common Mistake
Mixing up the two 'blue' alkalis: litmus goes BLUE in alkali, thymolphthalein also goes BLUE in alkali — but in ACID litmus is red while thymolphthalein is colourless. 'Colourless' is not the same as 'white' or 'no change recorded' — always write the word colourless.

📎 Key Points to Remember
• Litmus: red/blue. Methyl orange: red/yellow. Thymolphthalein: colourless/blue.
• One indicator = acid or alkali only; it cannot measure pH.

notes.heading: Universal Indicator and the pH Scale
notes.body:
📌 The pH scale
The pH scale runs from 0 to 14 and measures how acidic or alkaline an aqueous solution is:
• pH below 7 → acidic (the lower, the more acidic)
• pH 7 → neutral (pure water)
• pH above 7 → alkaline (the higher, the more alkaline)

🔑 Universal indicator
Universal indicator is a mixture of indicators that gives a different colour at each part of the scale: red/orange for strong and weak acids, green at pH 7, blue to purple for increasingly strong alkalis. It can be used as a solution or as indicator paper.

🔑 Measuring pH
• **Universal indicator** (paper or solution): compare the colour with a chart — quick but only to the nearest pH unit.
• **pH meter**: a probe giving an exact digital reading, e.g. pH 4.6.

⚠️ Common Mistake
Dipping indicator paper into the test solution. That contaminates the whole sample — put a drop of the solution onto the paper with a clean glass rod instead.

📎 Key Points to Remember
• pH < 7 acid, pH 7 neutral, pH > 7 alkali.
• Universal indicator estimates pH; a pH meter measures it exactly.

notes.heading: Acids, Bases and Alkalis: The Ions
notes.body:
📌 Definitions
• An **acid** is a substance that releases **hydrogen ions, H⁺(aq)**, when it dissolves in water. The (aq) matters — acids only show their acidic behaviour in aqueous solution.
• A **base** is a metal oxide or metal hydroxide that reacts with an acid to form a salt and water (it 'accepts' the acid's H⁺). Most bases are insoluble in water.
• An **alkali** is a base that IS soluble in water. In solution it releases **hydroxide ions, OH⁻(aq)**. Examples: sodium hydroxide NaOH, potassium hydroxide KOH, calcium hydroxide Ca(OH)₂, aqueous ammonia NH₃(aq).

🔑 How it works
Every alkali is a base, but not every base is an alkali: copper(II) oxide CuO is a base (it neutralises acids) but it is insoluble, so it is not an alkali. Solubility is the whole difference.

💡 Worked Example
Classify NaOH and CuO: both neutralise acids so both are bases; only NaOH dissolves in water releasing OH⁻, so only NaOH is an alkali.

⚠️ Common Mistake
Calling every base an alkali. If the oxide or hydroxide does not dissolve, there is no OH⁻(aq) in solution and 'alkali' is the wrong word.

📎 Key Points to Remember
• Acids are a source of H⁺(aq); alkalis are a source of OH⁻(aq).
• Alkali = soluble base.

notes.heading: Neutralisation: H⁺ + OH⁻ → H₂O
notes.body:
📌 The ionic equation — this IS Core
Every acid-alkali neutralisation is the same reaction at the ionic level:
**H⁺(aq) + OH⁻(aq) → H₂O(l)**
Whatever the acid and whatever the alkali, the hydrogen ions and hydroxide ions combine to form water. The other ions are spectators — they stay in solution and form the salt when the water is evaporated.

💡 Worked Example
HCl + NaOH → NaCl + H₂O and H₂SO₄ + 2KOH → K₂SO₄ + 2H₂O look different, but the essential change in both is H⁺(aq) + OH⁻(aq) → H₂O(l).

🔑 Why the state symbols matter
0620 mark schemes award the state symbols: (aq) for the ions dissolved in water, (l) for the water formed. Writing H⁺ + OH⁻ → H₂O without them can cost the mark.

⚠️ Common Mistake
Writing H⁺ + OH⁻ → H₂ + O₂ or H₂O₂. The ions join to make WATER — one H⁺ plus one OH⁻ gives exactly one H₂O.

📎 Key Points to Remember
• Neutralisation: H⁺(aq) + OH⁻(aq) → H₂O(l).
• The salt comes from the ions left over (the spectators).

notes.heading: Preparing a Pure Soluble Salt (Excess-Solid Method)
notes.body:
When the base or carbonate is INSOLUBLE, you cannot use an indicator to judge the endpoint — so you use excess solid instead. This method (acid + excess insoluble base or carbonate) is Core practical chemistry.

🔑 The method, step by step (making copper(II) sulfate from CuO + dilute H₂SO₄)
1. Measure the dilute acid into a beaker and **warm** it (warming speeds the reaction).
2. **Add the insoluble base in excess** — keep adding with stirring until no more dissolves and solid remains at the bottom. Excess guarantees ALL the acid has reacted, so the product is not contaminated with leftover acid.
3. **Filter** to remove the unreacted excess solid. The filtrate is a pure solution of the salt.
4. **Heat the filtrate to evaporate most of the water** until the solution is saturated (a drop cooled on a cold glass rod forms crystals).
5. **Leave to cool so crystals form**, then filter them off and dry between filter papers.

💡 Why not evaporate to dryness?
Boiling the solution dry would decompose or powder the crystals; stopping at saturation and cooling slowly gives large, pure crystals.

⚠️ Common Mistake
Forgetting the filtration step, or adding the salt 'until the indicator changes'. There is no indicator step in this method — the excess solid and the filter paper do that job.

📎 Key Points to Remember
• Excess solid → all acid used up → filter → evaporate to saturation → cool and crystallise.
• Works because the base/carbonate is insoluble, so the excess is easily removed.

illustration.alt: Five-step flow diagram for preparing a pure soluble salt from an acid and an excess of an insoluble base: warm the acid, add excess base until some remains undissolved, filter off the unreacted solid, evaporate the filtrate to saturation, then cool so pure crystals form.
illustration.caption: Excess insoluble base uses up all the acid; filtration removes the leftover solid; crystallisation gives the pure salt.

notes.heading: Solubility Rules for Common Salts
notes.body:
Whether a salt is soluble decides which preparation method is possible and which observations you should predict. The Core rules:

📌 Always soluble
• ALL sodium, potassium and ammonium salts.
• ALL nitrates.

📌 Mostly soluble — learn the exceptions
• **Chlorides** are soluble EXCEPT silver chloride AgCl and lead(II) chloride PbCl₂.
• **Sulfates** are soluble EXCEPT barium sulfate BaSO₄, lead(II) sulfate PbSO₄ (and calcium sulfate CaSO₄ is only sparingly soluble).

📌 Mostly insoluble — learn the exceptions
• **Carbonates** are insoluble EXCEPT sodium, potassium and ammonium carbonates.
• **Hydroxides** are insoluble EXCEPT sodium and potassium hydroxides (calcium hydroxide is sparingly soluble).

💡 Worked Example
Predict the solubility of KNO₃, AgCl and MgCO₃: KNO₃ — soluble (all nitrates and all potassium salts); AgCl — insoluble (the named chloride exception); MgCO₃ — insoluble (carbonates are insoluble unless Na/K/NH₄).

⚠️ Common Mistake
Thinking 'insoluble' means 'does not react'. Insoluble carbonates still react with acids — insolubility only describes whether the solid dissolves in water.

📎 Key Points to Remember
• Na⁺/K⁺/NH₄⁺ salts and nitrates: always soluble.
• Chloride exceptions: AgCl, PbCl₂. Sulfate exceptions: BaSO₄, PbSO₄ (CaSO₄ sparingly).
• Carbonates and hydroxides: insoluble except Na/K/NH₄.

flashcards.definition: Gives a salt + hydrogen. Only metals above hydrogen in the reactivity series react with dilute acids.
flashcards.example: Mg + H₂SO₄ → MgSO₄ + H₂; test the H₂ with a lighted splint — squeaky pop.

flashcards.definition: Gives a salt + water. Bases are metal oxides or metal hydroxides.
flashcards.example: CuO + 2HCl → CuCl₂ + H₂O (black copper(II) oxide dissolves in the warm acid).

flashcards.definition: Gives a salt + water + carbon dioxide. Effervescence is the observation.
flashcards.example: CaCO₃ + 2HNO₃ → Ca(NO₃)₂ + H₂O + CO₂; the CO₂ turns limewater milky.

flashcards.definition: The acid decides the salt name: hydrochloric → chloride, sulfuric → sulfate, nitric → nitrate. The metal gives the first word.
flashcards.example: Zinc + sulfuric acid → zinc sulfate; zinc + hydrochloric acid → zinc chloride.

flashcards.definition: Red in acidic solution, blue in alkaline solution.
flashcards.example: Vinegar turns blue litmus paper red.

flashcards.definition: Red in acidic solution, yellow in alkaline solution.
flashcards.example: Sodium hydroxide solution turns methyl orange yellow.

flashcards.definition: Colourless in acidic solution, blue in alkaline solution.
flashcards.example: In dilute hydrochloric acid thymolphthalein is colourless; in limewater it is blue.

flashcards.definition: Runs 0-14: below 7 is acidic, 7 is neutral, above 7 is alkaline. Measured with universal indicator or a pH meter.
flashcards.example: Universal indicator is green at pH 7; a pH meter reads exact values like 4.6.

flashcards.definition: A source of hydrogen ions, H⁺(aq), in aqueous solution.
flashcards.example: HCl dissolves in water releasing H⁺(aq) and Cl⁻(aq).

flashcards.definition: A soluble base — a source of hydroxide ions, OH⁻(aq), in aqueous solution.
flashcards.example: NaOH, KOH and aqueous ammonia are alkalis; insoluble CuO is a base but not an alkali.

flashcards.definition: H⁺(aq) + OH⁻(aq) → H₂O(l) — the essential reaction in every acid-alkali neutralisation.
flashcards.example: In HCl + NaOH → NaCl + H₂O, the Na⁺ and Cl⁻ are spectators; the real change is H⁺ + OH⁻ → H₂O.

flashcards.definition: All Na/K/NH₄ salts and all nitrates are soluble; chlorides except AgCl/PbCl₂; sulfates except BaSO₄/PbSO₄; carbonates insoluble except Na/K/NH₄.
flashcards.example: AgCl is an insoluble chloride; K₂CO₃ is a soluble carbonate.

questions.stem: What colour is litmus in an acidic solution?
questions.explanation: Litmus is red in acid and blue in alkali. Yellow belongs to methyl orange in alkali and colourless to thymolphthalein in acid.

questions.stem: Dilute hydrochloric acid is added to sodium carbonate. What are the products?
questions.explanation: Acid + carbonate → salt + water + carbon dioxide: 2HCl + Na₂CO₃ → 2NaCl + H₂O + CO₂. Hydrogen is only made when an acid reacts with a metal.

questions.stem: A solution has a pH of 1. The solution is:
questions.explanation: pH 1 is far below 7, so the solution is strongly acidic. Weak acids sit closer to 7 (pH 4-6); pH 7 is neutral.

questions.stem: A few drops of methyl orange are added to sodium hydroxide solution. What colour is seen?
questions.explanation: Sodium hydroxide is an alkali, and methyl orange is yellow in alkali (red in acid). Blue would be litmus or thymolphthalein in alkali — not methyl orange.

questions.stem: Black copper(II) oxide powder is stirred into warm dilute sulfuric acid until no more dissolves. What is in the solution?
questions.explanation: Acid + base (metal oxide) → salt + water: CuO + H₂SO₄ → CuSO₄ + H₂O. Sulfuric acid gives a sulfate; no gas is made because CuO is a base, not a metal or a carbonate.

questions.stem: What colour is thymolphthalein in dilute hydrochloric acid?
questions.explanation: Thymolphthalein is colourless in acid and blue in alkali. Do not confuse it with litmus, which is red in acid.

questions.stem: Which ionic equation summarises every acid-alkali neutralisation?
questions.explanation: In every neutralisation the hydrogen ions from the acid and the hydroxide ions from the alkali form water: H⁺(aq) + OH⁻(aq) → H₂O(l). The other ions are spectators and form the salt.

questions.stem: In the excess-solid method for making copper(II) sulfate crystals from copper(II) oxide and dilute sulfuric acid, why is the copper(II) oxide added in excess?
choices: To make the reaction mixture turn blue
To neutralise the carbon dioxide produced
To make sure all the acid reacts, so no acid is left to contaminate the salt — the unreacted solid is then removed by filtration
To increase the concentration of the sulfuric acid
questions.explanation: Excess insoluble base guarantees the acid is completely used up. Because CuO is insoluble, the leftover solid is simply filtered off, leaving a pure copper(II) sulfate solution to crystallise.

questions.stem: Universal indicator turns green when added to a solution. What is the pH of the solution?
questions.explanation: Universal indicator is green at pH 7 — neutral. Reds and oranges show acids; blues and purples show alkalis.

questions.stem: Which of these salts is INSOLUBLE in water?
questions.explanation: All nitrates, all sodium salts and most chlorides are soluble. Barium sulfate is one of the named insoluble sulfate exceptions (with lead(II) sulfate).

questions.stem: All aqueous acids show acidic behaviour because they release which ion in solution?
questions.explanation: Acids are a source of hydrogen ions, H⁺(aq). OH⁻ is the ion released by alkalis — the opposite class.

questions.stem: A student has warmed dilute sulfuric acid and stirred in excess copper(II) oxide until solid remains undissolved. What is the correct NEXT step in preparing pure copper(II) sulfate crystals?
choices: Filter off the unreacted copper(II) oxide
Add universal indicator to check for neutralisation
Boil the mixture until all the water has evaporated
questions.explanation: Once excess solid remains, all the acid has reacted. The next step is filtration to remove the unreacted CuO; only then is the filtrate evaporated to saturation and left to crystallise. Boiling to dryness ruins the crystals.

questions.stem: Which statement about bases and alkalis is correct?
choices: An alkali is a soluble base that releases OH⁻(aq) in water; insoluble bases such as CuO are not alkalis
Alkalis release H⁺ ions in solution
questions.explanation: Bases (metal oxides and hydroxides) neutralise acids, but only the soluble ones — the alkalis — release hydroxide ions in solution. CuO neutralises acids but is insoluble, so it is a base, not an alkali.

questions.stem: Which of the following is an alkali?
questions.explanation: An alkali is a SOLUBLE base. Sodium hydroxide dissolves in water releasing OH⁻(aq). Copper(II) oxide and iron(III) oxide are insoluble bases; calcium carbonate is a carbonate, not a hydroxide base-alkali.

questions.stem: A gas produced when an acid reacts with a carbonate is bubbled through limewater. What result confirms the gas is carbon dioxide?
questions.explanation: CO₂ turns limewater milky (cloudy) — the standard test. A squeaky pop is the test for hydrogen, which comes from acid + metal, not acid + carbonate.
